The majority of New Zealanders (approximately 80%) born in the 1970s report using cannabis at least once, despite its illegal status.

9-20% of past-year users were at risk of developing a cannabis dependence syndrome that impaired psychological, social and/or occupational functioning.

There were negative psychiatric consequences for a subset of the population who began using cannabis in early/mid-adolescence, particularly in terms of developing psychosis (the risk appeared to be highest for those with a genetic predisposition), and to a lesser degree for depression.

There was a consistent dose–response relation between increasing levels of, and/or persistence of cannabis use and a range of deleterious health outcomes including loss of cognitive capacity, increased respiratory symptoms and impaired lung function, compromised educational achievement and employment history, as well as a host of negative social outcomes.

The majority of cannabis users did so with little or no harm. In contrast, a non-trivial minority of the population (approximately 5%–10%) were at heightened risk because they:

  • used cannabis on more days than not
  • had become cannabis dependent
  • began using cannabis during mid-adolescence and persisted well into adulthood

There have also been studies that show women reported greater withdrawal intensity and worse withdrawal symptoms, predominantly due to physiological and mood symptoms. Women were more likely to have lifetime panic disorder and current agoraphobia, and reported more days of poor physical health and cannabis-related medical problems. Women reporting chronic pain had greater mean pain scores than men with chronic pain.

Even though this is a website where we love smoking weed, its important to listen to the facts and data from studies that are coming out. Marijuana has been around for approx 5000 years but only in the last few years have we had to scientific advancements as well as computing and people power to research cannabis to new extents. These studies show cannabis dependencies can arise and how it affects us. Its important to regulate how youre smoking because I get it. Ive been smoking almost daily for 2 years now. Its been a coping mechanism for me after work and with friends. When my head gets to busy and crazy it just feels so much better to be high. But I've already seen the side effects that long term use has. And time goes so fast, you dont think your'e smoking that much and then boom you struggle to go longer than a day without smoking and you have so many excuses for not quitting. I can't get to sleep without it... it helps me destress... im quitting ciggies... im only doing it with friends(who you see every day)... Depression is something i've struggles with since i was a child. To be honest, weed has helped me a lot over these past few years. I am a full advocate for using weed for depression. But since weed is still criminalized in new zealand we cant control the cbd or thc levels we are smoking. Criminalization also means schools cant teach drug education which means you only learn about how to use drugs safely through trial and error. And in the end; weed is still a drug and we can suffer from drug addictions and need access to help, even if its just assistance controlling the levels of weed we are consuming in the most healthy, optimized way for each person, even depending on their existing tolerances, physical and medical illnesses, metabolism, and gender.
